Date: 2026-08-02

Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Alex Moreno (Zenith - Head of Product); Maya Patel (Zenith - Eng Lead); Samir Khan (Zenith - CTO)
summary: AE intro + product overview; SE demo of Hosted API for chat/text generation focusing on streaming, key params (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), retries/backoff patterns and SDK examples. Discussed security (SSO/SAML, SOC2), data residency, and pilot next steps.
transcript: [00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey team, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Alex Moreno: Doing well, thanks. Excited to see the hosted API demo — we're looking at chat and text gen for our product assistant.

[00:14] Priya Nair: Great. Quick agenda — we'll do a short qual check, high level hosted API overview, then a live demo showing streaming responses, param tuning (temp/top_p/max_tokens), and best practices for retries. We'll leave time for Q&A.

[00:26] Samir Khan: Sounds good — our main constraints are latency under 200ms for short responses, data controls for PII, and predictable cost. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated for an initial launch.
[00:36] Jordan Lee: Perfect, that's helpful. Timeline?
[00:38] Maya Patel: We're aiming to ship a beta in Q4, pilot with 5k daily active users. Security review early next week would be ideal.

[00:44] Priya Nair: Good to know. Ok jumping into the demo — I'll share my screen. We're going to start with the basic chat/text endpoint using curl and then the JS SDK for streaming. Note: links to the quickstart and benchmark sheet are in the calendar invite (link: https://redwood.dev/quickstart and spreadsheet: https://redwood.dev/benchmarks).

[01:10] Priya Nair: Example curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-1","input":"Hello, summarize our meeting"}' — that's the synchronous call. For streaming we use Server-Sent Events or chunked responses; here's a Node example using our SDK...

[01:35] Priya Nair: // pseudocode
const stream = client.responses.stream({ model:'redwood-chat-1', input:'Write a friendly greeting', temperature:0.7, max_tokens:120 })
stream.on('data', chunk => process.stdout.write(chunk.text))
stream.on('end', () => console.log('done'))
[02:05] Alex Moreno: So streaming will push partial tokens as they are generated? That helps perceived latency, right?

[02:12] Priya Nair: Exactly. Instead of waiting for full 300 tokens, you get the first tokens within ~50-100ms depending on model and sequence length. For your 200ms SLO on short responses, streaming with a smaller max_tokens and model selection is key.
[02:28] Samir Khan: What about token billing with streaming? Do we get charged per token as usual?
[02:33] Jordan Lee: Yes per-token billing applies; streaming doesn't change unit economics, but perceived latency improves. We can show cost per 1k tokens in the pricing sheet.

[02:45] Priya Nair: Now params — temperature controls randomness, 0.0-1.0; top_p is nucleus sampling. For deterministic responses we recommend temp 0-0.2 and top_p 0.8-1.0. Use max_tokens to limit length and 'stop' tokens for structured outputs.
[03:08] Maya Patel: Do you have guidance for few-shot prompts vs system messages? We're doing product-specific persona and don't want hallucinations.

[03:15] Priya Nair: System messages for global behavior, few-shot examples for task-specific constraints. Also we offer reranking and safety filters — you can run a lightweight safety check post-generation or use our built-in moderation model. For hallucinations, we recommend grounding with the user's context and retrieval if needed.
[03:36] Alex Moreno: Can you demo retries? We had issues with 503s when upstream GPUs were busy and naive retries doubled user-visible latency.

[03:42] Priya Nair: Yes — Redwood exposes HTTP 429/503 semantics and we recommend idempotency keys for non-chat requests or a request identifier header 'X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key' so retries are safe. Our client has exponential backoff built-in. Example: retry with jitter, backoff 200ms->600ms->1.8s and abort after 4 attempts. For streaming, if a connection drops you can resume with the last committed token position in some model variants; otherwise we re-request with the same idempotency key and dedupe on the service side.
[04:20] Samir Khan: Resume is model-dependent?

[04:22] Priya Nair: Correct. Not every quantized variant supports resume; we fall back to restart and can stitch using prefix cache on our side to reduce compute. There was a typo in some of our docs where 'KV cache' got transcribed as 'K-V cash' — ignore that :)
[04:36] Alex Moreno: For your hosted offering, what are the SLA and uptime?

[04:40] Jordan Lee: Hosted API has 99.9% uptime for paid tiers, and we provide latency targets per model class in the performance profiles. Dedicated gives stronger throughput guarantees and isolation. We'll include SLA details in the doc bundle I send.
[04:54] Maya Patel: Security — SSO/SAML, audit logs, data retention, and encryption at rest?

[04:58] Jordan Lee: We support SSO via SAML and OIDC, RBAC at org/team/route levels, SOC 2 Type II compliance, and integration with KMS for customer-managed keys on Dedicated and Private. Hosted keeps transient logs only per your retention settings; we can arrange different retention policies for enterprise plans.

[05:18] Priya Nair: For data residency, we have region pinning and can route requests to EU or US regions. For the pilot, most customers use hosted with strict encryption and retention settings; Private deployment is available if you need air-gapped or on-prem.
[05:33] Alex Moreno: Good. Back to the demo — can you show a real example of a short chat response with streaming and then show param changes?

[05:38] Priya Nair: Yep. I'm going to invoke a chat with model 'redwood-chat-1' and temperature 0.2, max_tokens 60, stop=['\n\n']. Streaming coming in... [screen shows partial tokens arriving]. You can see the first 6 tokens arrive quickly, then subsequent chunks. Now I'll bump temp to 0.8 to show variation — you can see outputs are more diverse. That's a quick way to tune creativity vs determinism.
[06:12] Alex Moreno: Nice. How do you recommend A/B testing parameter sets?

[06:16] Priya Nair: Use per-route configs in the Console — you can create two routes with the same prompt but different params and traffic split. Console has per-route metrics: latency, tokens/req, cost, and quality signals if you hook up eval sets.
[06:31] Maya Patel: Do you have SDKs for retriable requests and streaming in Python?
[06:58] Samir Khan: On cost, can you show ballpark numbers for our expected load? We estimate 5k DAU, avg 100 tokens per session, 2 calls/session.

[07:06] Jordan Lee: We'll run a quick calc in the pricing sheet but roughly: tokens/day = 5k * 2 * 100 = 1M tokens/day; multiply by per-1k token rate in the sheet. We'll send a tailored estimate after we see your traffic shape and whether batching/caching applies.
[07:24] Alex Moreno: About caching — you mentioned prefix/KV caching earlier. How does that affect freshness?

[07:29] Priya Nair: Prefix caching caches model KV for repeated prefixes (good for canned prompts). KV cache hits reduce compute and latency but you need to consider staleness if prompt includes recent context. Our Optimize toolkit suggests cache TTLs per route and shows cache hit metrics in Console.
[07:46] Maya Patel: Any common pitfalls when moving from PoC to prod?

[07:50] Priya Nair: Yes — (1) not setting proper stop tokens leading to long responses, (2) insufficient idempotency keys causing duplicate side-effects, (3) ignoring tokenization differences for costs. Also misconfigured retries can amplify load during partial outages.
[08:05] Alex Moreno: You mentioned structured outputs — can we enforce JSON output?

[08:09] Priya Nair: Yes — use system messages and a strict schema with a JSON validator, or use our structured output feature where the model is constrained and the service validates outputs. We also support function/tool calling patterns to limit hallucinations.
[08:24] Samir Khan: On the enterprise side, how is logging/auditing surfaced?

[08:29] Jordan Lee: Console exposes request-level logs, token-level cost breakdowns, and we can stream audit logs to your SIEM via our integrations. For Dedicated and Private you can ship logs to your storage and pair with our tracing hooks.

[08:44] Priya Nair: Quick note: sometimes our transcription of internal demos shows product names a bit off — you might see 'Redwood Dedicated' transcribed weirdly in notes; ignore those typos. Back to questions?
[08:56] Maya Patel: How long does it take to get pilot credentials for hosted?
[08:59] Jordan Lee: We can provision a trial org within 24-48 hours. For SSO or custom retention policies it might take a few extra days.
[09:05] Alex Moreno: For benchmarks, can you run a run with our sample payloads and target latency SLO of 200ms?

[09:10] Priya Nair: Yes — Priya will run bench on our hosted perf profiles using your sample queries. We'll test with streaming and non-streaming to show p50/p95. We'll include cost per 1k tokens and recommended model variants (e.g., redwood-chat-1, redwood-text-lite).
[09:26] Samir Khan: Any limits we should be aware of (rate limits)?

[09:29] Jordan Lee: Default rate limits exist per API key; for production we normally raise limits or recommend Dedicated for high QPS. We also support per-route throttling so you can protect downstream systems.

[09:40] Priya Nair: Quick live code: I'll show retry logic with exponential backoff and idempotency header in Node. // pseudocode\nclient.responses.create({idempotencyKey:'uuid', ...}).catch(err => retryWithBackoff(err))
[09:58] Alex Moreno: If we hit rate limit, is there a header that tells us when to retry?
[10:02] Priya Nair: Yes we return Retry-After and a recommended backoff; client SDKs honor that header automatically.
[10:08] Maya Patel: Can you run the bench with our long-tail conversational prompts? Some are 800-1200 tokens.

[10:13] Priya Nair: We'll include both short and long context tests; note long contexts change kernel selection and sometimes fall back to quantized variants which can impact latency. We'll surface that in the perf report.
[10:27] Samir Khan: For the pilot, we'd want predictable pricing. Do you offer committed plans?
[10:32] Jordan Lee: Yes Reserved capacity for Dedicated and committed usage discounts for hosted. We'll include options in the pricing doc I send.
[10:40] Alex Moreno: Anything else about observability?

[10:43] Priya Nair: Console has per-route dashboards, trace IDs you can pass in headers for correlation, token-level breakdowns, error analysis. Also Redwood Optimize surfaces model/quantization recommendations based on your traffic.
[11:00] Maya Patel: Is there a quick way to revert model rollouts if quality regresses?

[11:04] Priya Nair: Yes — Console supports canary rollouts and automatic rollback based on perf or QA signals. You can set automatic fallback to a previous model or to a cheaper variant if latencies spike.
[11:18] Alex Moreno: What about data egress for EU users?
[11:21] Jordan Lee: We have EU region pinning and can ensure requests and logs stay in-region. For strict residency we recommend Private deployment.
[11:28] Maya Patel: Let's talk about a POC. What would you need from us?

[11:31] Jordan Lee: Sample query corpus, expected traffic profile, security requirements (SSO/KMS), and a POC success definition — e.g., p95 latency < 500ms for long-form, <200ms for short-form, and cost per DAU below X. We'll draft a POC plan.
[11:46] Alex Moreno: We'll share that by Wednesday. Any blockers on your side to start?
[11:50] Priya Nair: None. We'll need an API key for the trial and a sample dataset. We'll run bench and share results in 5 business days.

[12:00] Jordan Lee: Quick recap: we'll send pricing + SSO docs (Jordan), run benchmarks with your samples (Priya), and you send sample corpus (Maya). I'll put the action items in CRM and send invite for follow-up next week.
[12:15] Samir Khan: One last question — do you have a reference customer in fintech/ops?
[12:19] Jordan Lee: Yes, we have a few references; I'll include two case studies in the email. One used hosted initially and migrated to Dedicated for peak holiday traffic.
[12:30] Alex Moreno: Great. Thanks for the demo — that was helpful. We'll follow up with the corpus and we expect the security team may have more questions on SSO and SOC2.
[12:38] Priya Nair: Happy to set up a security deep-dive with our compliance lead. I'll include available times in the follow-up.
[12:45] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll email next steps and the benchmark spreadsheet shortly. Talk soon.
[12:50] Meeting ends
